lessons.title: Module 11 Lesson 1: Understanding Your Market and Customer Base
lessons.body: Welcome to Module 11 of Small Shop and Market Trading. In this first lesson we focus on the foundation of every successful trading business: knowing exactly who your customers are and what they need. In many African markets, from Kibera to Kano, from Accra's Makola to Johannesburg's taxi ranks, the traders who thrive are not necessarily those with the most capital. They are the ones who understand their customers deeply. Your shop or stall is not just a place to sell goods. It is a service point for a community. Your job is to solve problems for that community at a price they can afford and in a way that earns their trust. Start by mapping your catchment area. Who walks past your shop every day? Are they workers going to a factory, mothers buying food for the evening meal, students from a nearby school, or travellers waiting for transport? Each group has different buying times, different budgets, and different product needs. A trader near a bus stage should stock quick snacks, airtime, and small sachets of water. A trader near a residential area should stock cooking oil, maize flour, soap, and school exercise books. Write down the main groups you see. Then for each group, list what they buy, when they buy, and how much they typically spend. This simple exercise will change how you order stock. Next, study your competition. Do not fear other traders. Learn from them. What are they selling that moves fast? What are they always running out of? What complaints do customers make about them? Maybe the nearby shopkeeper is rude, or closes early, or only sells in large quantities. These are your opportunities. You can open earlier, smile more, sell in smaller affordable units, or offer credit to trusted customers. In African markets, relationships are currency. A customer who feels respected will walk past three other shops to buy from you. Now think about pricing. Many small traders price by guessing. Instead, use a simple cost-plus method. Know your landed cost for every item, including transport, packaging, and any market fees. Add a markup that covers your time and risk. For fast-moving staples like sugar or rice, your markup may be thin because customers know the price everywhere. For unique or convenient items, you can charge more. Always calculate your break-even point. If your monthly rent is 500, your transport is 200, and your other costs are 300, you need at least 1000 in gross profit before you pay yourself anything. Divide that by your average profit per sale to know how many sales you need each day. This number keeps you focused. Customer service is your cheapest marketing. Greet every person who enters. Learn names. Remember what they bought last time. If a customer asks for an item you do not have, write it down and try to stock it next time. This shows you listen. In many African communities, word of mouth travels faster than any radio advert. One happy customer can bring five neighbours. One rude encounter can cost you ten. Keep a small notebook or use a basic phone app to record customer requests and feedback. Also, watch your busiest hours. If most sales happen between 6am and 9am, make sure you are fully stocked and ready before 6am. If evening sales are strong, stay open later even if it means resting in the afternoon. Your schedule should follow your customers, not your comfort. Finally, think about trust and credit. Many customers will ask for goods on credit, especially near month-end. Credit can build loyalty, but it can also destroy your business if mismanaged. Set clear rules. Only give credit to regular customers you know. Keep a written record of every debt, with date, amount, and agreed repayment time. Never give credit for more than a small percentage of your total stock value. If someone fails to pay, stop giving credit until they clear the old balance. Be firm but respectful. In this lesson, you have learned to map your customers, study competitors, price with knowledge, serve with respect, and manage credit wisely. These habits separate a struggling stall from a growing business. In the next lesson, we will look at stock selection and sourcing so you always have what your customers want at the best possible cost.

lessons.title: Module 11 Lesson 2: Smart Stock Selection and Sourcing
lessons.body: In this lesson we dive into the lifeblood of your trading business: stock. What you stock, how much you stock, and where you buy it determines whether you make profit or tie up your money in goods that gather dust. Many small shop owners in Africa fail not because they lack customers, but because they buy the wrong items, buy too much of slow movers, or buy from expensive sources. We will fix that with practical steps. First, classify your stock into three groups: fast movers, medium movers, and slow movers. Fast movers are items you sell every day, such as bread, milk, airtime, cooking oil, or single cigarettes. Medium movers sell a few times a week, like washing powder, tinned fish, or batteries. Slow movers might sell once a month, like special spices, tools, or seasonal items. Your money should follow the fast movers. Never let slow movers eat more than 20 percent of your stock budget. If an item has not sold in 30 days, consider discounting it to recover cash, even if you make little profit. Cash tied up in dead stock cannot buy the bread that customers want today. Next, understand your stock turnover. Turnover is how many times you sell and replace your stock in a period. If you buy 100 loaves of bread and sell them in two days, your turnover is fast. If you buy 50 bags of cement and sell them over three months, your turnover is slow. Fast turnover means your money works harder. Aim to keep your shelves full of items that turn over quickly. A simple rule: if you would not buy it again next week, do not buy a large quantity this week. Sourcing is the next skill. Where you buy determines your cost, your quality, and your reliability. In many African cities, you have options: local wholesalers, open-air markets, direct from farmers or producers, and sometimes regional distributors. Compare at least three suppliers for your top ten items. Ask about price, minimum order, delivery, and credit terms. A supplier who delivers to your shop may be worth a slightly higher price because you save transport and time. A supplier who gives you one week to pay can help your cash flow, but only if you trust the quality. Build relationships with suppliers. Visit them regularly. Pay on time when you can. When you are a reliable buyer, you can negotiate better prices, get first pick of fresh stock, and sometimes receive extra goods on credit during tough times. In African markets, trust between trader and supplier is as important as price. Also, consider joining a buying group with other small traders. When five or ten shops combine their orders, they can buy at wholesale rates that none could access alone. This is common in countries like Kenya, Ghana, and Nigeria, where trader associations negotiate directly with manufacturers. If no group exists, start one with nearby trusted traders. You do not need a formal office. A simple WhatsApp group can coordinate orders and share transport costs. Quality control is critical. Customers will not return if your rice has stones, your milk is expired, or your phone chargers fail after one week. Always inspect goods before you pay. Check expiry dates. Open a sample carton. Smell and touch fresh produce. If a supplier sells you poor quality, return it immediately or refuse it. Do not accept the excuse that all sales are final. Your reputation is worth more than a cheap deal. For perishable goods like tomatoes, fish, or vegetables, you need a different approach. Buy smaller quantities more often. Use cold storage if available, even a simple cooler with ice. Sell the oldest stock first. If you see spoilage starting, reduce the price immediately to recover something rather than losing everything. In many markets, the last hour of trading is when smart traders discount remaining perishables to avoid total loss. Record keeping is your guide. Keep a simple stock book or use a phone app. Write down what you bought, when, from whom, at what price, and what you sold. At the end of each week, review which items made the most profit and which sat idle. Adjust your next order based on facts, not feelings. Many traders order the same things out of habit. Break that habit. Order what sells. Finally, think about seasonality. Demand changes during school terms, religious festivals, rainy seasons, and harvest times. Stock more exercise books in January. Stock more food items during Ramadan or Christmas. Stock umbrellas and raincoats when the rains come. If you plan ahead, you can buy these items before prices rise and sell them when everyone needs them. In this lesson, you have learned to classify stock, watch turnover, compare suppliers, join buying groups, control quality, manage perishables, keep records, and plan for seasons. These practices will keep your shelves profitable and your cash flowing. In the next lesson, we will focus on pricing, profit, and managing your money day to day.

lessons.title: Module 11 Lesson 3: Pricing, Profit, and Daily Cash Management
lessons.body: Money is the blood of your business. If it stops flowing, the business dies. In this lesson we focus on three connected skills: setting prices that earn profit, calculating your true costs, and managing cash every single day. Many small traders in Africa work hard but stay poor because they do not separate business money from personal money, do not know their real profit, and do not plan for slow days. We will change that. Start with pricing. There are three common methods. The first is cost-plus pricing. You take the cost of the item, add transport and other direct costs, then add a profit margin. For example, if a carton of soap costs 1000 and transport is 100, your landed cost is 1100. If you want a 20 percent margin, you sell the carton for 1320. This method is simple and safe. The second is market pricing. You check what other traders charge and set your price close to theirs. This works for common goods where customers know the price. But be careful: if you simply match the lowest price, you may be selling at a loss. Always know your cost before you match anyone. The third is value-based pricing. You charge more because you offer something extra: convenience, credit, delivery, or a better location. A shop open at 5am when others are closed can charge a little more for bread and milk. A trader who delivers to homes can charge a premium. Value-based pricing works when customers see the benefit. Whatever method you use, calculate your break-even point. Break-even is the number of sales you need to cover all your costs. List your fixed costs each month: rent, licenses, phone data, security, and any wages. Add your variable costs: transport, packaging, and market fees. Suppose your fixed costs are 800 and your average profit per sale is 20. You need 40 sales just to break even. Every sale after that is profit. Knowing this number helps you decide whether to open on a slow day or stay home. Now, cash management. The biggest mistake small traders make is mixing business cash with household cash. You buy stock with 5000, sell it for 6000, then use 2000 for school fees and 1000 for food. Soon you cannot restock. The business shrinks. To avoid this, separate your money. Keep a business cash box or a mobile money wallet used only for business. Pay yourself a fixed small salary each week, and take extra profit only after you have restocked and covered all business costs. Record every sale and every expense. Even a notebook with two columns, money in and money out, is enough. At the end of each day, count your cash. Compare it to your records. If there is a shortage, find out why. Maybe you gave credit and forgot to write it down, or maybe you took money for personal use. Honesty with yourself is essential. Manage credit carefully. Credit sales are not cash until the customer pays. If you sell 3000 worth of goods on credit, you cannot use that money to buy new stock. Keep credit small and track it. Set a rule: no customer owes more than a certain amount, say 500 or 1000. Write the date, name, item, and amount. Follow up politely but firmly. If a customer avoids you, stop giving credit. Also, build a small emergency fund. In trading, shocks happen: a supplier raises prices, a customer disappears with debt, a family emergency arises. If you have no savings, you may be forced to sell stock at a loss or borrow expensively. Aim to save even 50 or 100 per day in a separate place. Over a month, that becomes a cushion. Use mobile money savings or a trusted savings group, known in many countries as a chama, susu, or stokvel. These groups also provide discipline and sometimes emergency loans. Watch your cash flow, not just your profit. Profit is what remains after all costs. Cash flow is the timing of money in and out. You can be profitable on paper but run out of cash if customers buy on credit or if you hold too much slow stock. Always keep enough cash to restock your fast movers. If you must choose between buying a slow-moving item with high margin and a fast-moving item with low margin, choose the fast mover. It brings cash back sooner. Review your prices regularly. Costs change. Transport fares rise. Supplier prices increase. If you do not adjust, your margin disappears. But do not raise prices carelessly. Explain to customers when necessary. Offer smaller sizes or bundles to keep prices affordable. For example, instead of raising the price of a 2kg bag of rice, introduce a 1kg pack at half the price. Customers appreciate options. Finally, separate your business records from your memory. Memory fails. Records do not. At the end of each week, calculate your gross profit, your expenses, and your net profit. Ask yourself: which items made the most money? Which days were strongest? Where did cash leak? Use these answers to plan the next week. In this lesson, you have learned pricing methods, break-even analysis, cash separation, credit control, emergency savings, cash flow, and regular review. These habits turn a busy stall into a stable business. In the next lesson, we will cover customer relationships, marketing, and growing your sales without spending much money.

lessons.title: Module 11 Lesson 4: Customer Relationships, Marketing, and Sales Growth
lessons.body: In this lesson we focus on growing your sales by building strong customer relationships and using low-cost marketing that works in African markets. Many traders believe marketing means expensive radio adverts or printed banners. In reality, the most powerful marketing for a small shop is word of mouth, visible presence, and consistent good service. Let us start with relationships. Your customers are not just people who give you money. They are your neighbours, your community, and your best salespeople. Treat every customer as a long-term relationship, not a one-time transaction. Greet people warmly. Use local languages where possible. Ask about their family, their work, their day. This is not fake friendliness. It is genuine respect, and it builds loyalty. Remember details. If Mama Aisha always buys milk and bread on Saturday morning, have it ready. If Baba Kofi prefers a certain brand of soap, keep it in stock. When a customer feels known, they will not easily go elsewhere. Handle complaints well. Every business makes mistakes. Maybe you sold expired milk, or gave the wrong change, or ran out of a popular item. What matters is how you respond. Apologise sincerely. Replace the item or refund the money without argument. A customer whose complaint is resolved well often becomes more loyal than one who never had a problem. Never argue in front of other customers. Take the conversation aside. Protect the customer's dignity. Now, marketing. Your first marketing tool is your shop itself. Make it visible. Clean the front. Arrange goods neatly. Use bright colours or simple hand-painted signs. In many African markets, a clean, well-lit stall attracts more customers than a dark, cluttered one. If you can, paint your shop name and what you sell. A simple board saying Fresh Bread Daily or Airtime All Networks tells people what you offer. Your second tool is consistency. Open at the same time every day. Keep the same prices for regular customers. Be reliable. When people know they can count on you, they plan their shopping around you. Your third tool is word of mouth. Ask happy customers to tell others. You can encourage this gently. Give a small extra item to a customer who brings a friend. Offer a loyalty card made from a simple piece of cardboard. After ten purchases, the customer gets a small discount or free item. This costs little but builds habit. Your fourth tool is mobile phone marketing. Most customers have phones. Collect phone numbers with permission. Send a simple message when new stock arrives, when prices drop, or when you have a special offer. Do not spam. One or two messages a week is enough. You can also use WhatsApp status to show photos of fresh produce or new arrivals. This is free and reaches many people quickly. Your fifth tool is partnerships. Team up with other businesses that serve the same customers. A barber, a tailor, or a mobile money agent near you can recommend your shop, and you can recommend theirs. You can also supply small quantities to food vendors, salons, or offices. Selling in bulk to a few regular business customers can stabilise your income. Now, sales growth. There are three ways to grow: sell more to existing customers, sell to new customers, and sell higher-margin items. To sell more to existing customers, use bundling. Instead of selling rice alone, sell a cooking pack with rice, oil, and salt at a small discount. Instead of selling airtime alone, offer a bundle with a phone charger. Bundles increase the average sale. To attract new customers, improve your visibility. Stand outside during peak hours. Call out your offers politely. Give free samples of a new product. Offer a small opening discount for first-time buyers. To sell higher-margin items, place them near the counter where customers wait. A customer who came for bread may also buy a cold drink or a sweet if it is visible. Train yourself to suggest one additional item politely. Would you like a cold soda with that? This simple question increases sales. Also, watch your busy and slow periods. During slow hours, use the time to arrange stock, clean, and plan. During busy hours, focus fully on serving quickly. Do not chat with friends while customers wait. Time is money for your customers too. Finally, measure your growth. Count your customers each day or each week. Track your average sale value. If you had 50 customers yesterday and 60 today, you are growing. If your average sale was 100 and now it is 120, you are growing. Use these numbers to set simple targets. Maybe next month you want 10 percent more customers or 10 percent higher average sale. Write the target down. Review it weekly. In this lesson, you have learned to build relationships, handle complaints, use your shop as marketing, encourage word of mouth, use mobile phones, form partnerships, bundle products, increase average sales, and measure growth. These actions cost little but can double your income over time. In the next and final lesson, we will cover record keeping, planning, and building long-term resilience for your trading business.

lessons.title: Module 11 Lesson 5: Record Keeping, Planning, and Long-Term Resilience
lessons.body: Welcome to the final lesson of Module 11. Here we bring everything together with the habits that keep a small shop or market stall alive for years, not just months. These habits are record keeping, planning, adapting to change, and building resilience. Many traders start well but fail because they do not write things down, do not plan ahead, and cannot survive shocks. You will learn simple, practical systems that work even if you have little education or no smartphone. Start with record keeping. You do not need complicated accounting. You need four simple records. First, a sales record. Every day, write down total sales and the main items sold. If you can, note which items sold best. Second, an expense record. Write down every payment: stock, transport, rent, airtime, food, and personal withdrawals. Third, a stock record. Note what you bought, when, and at what price. Fourth, a debt record. List every customer who owes you, the amount, the date, and when they promised to pay. Use a hardcover notebook and a pen. Keep it in a safe place. At the end of each day, spend ten minutes filling it in. At the end of each week, review it. Ask three questions: Did I make a profit this week? Which items made the most money? Where did I waste money? These questions will guide your decisions. If you have a smartphone, you can use simple apps or even a spreadsheet. But the notebook is enough. The important thing is consistency. A record kept daily is worth more than a perfect system used once a month. Next, planning. A trader without a plan reacts to whatever happens. A trader with a plan prepares for what is likely to happen. Make three plans: a daily plan, a weekly plan, and a monthly plan. Your daily plan includes opening time, restocking needs, and any customer follow-ups. Your weekly plan includes supplier visits, stock review, and cash counting. Your monthly plan includes rent payment, license renewal, savings deposit, and a review of your best and worst items. Also plan for seasons. Know the school calendar, the rainy season, the harvest, and the festivals in your area. Stock ahead for these times. If you know that demand for umbrellas rises in April, buy them in March when prices are lower. If you know that school uniforms sell in December, order them early. Planning turns you from a follower of the market into a leader in your niche. Now, adapting to change. Markets change. Customers change. Technology changes. A trader who refuses to adapt will be left behind. In recent years, mobile money has changed how people pay. If you do not accept mobile money, you lose customers. If you do not use a phone to order stock or communicate with suppliers, you waste time. If you do not watch new products that young people want, you miss sales. Stay curious. Talk to customers about what they want. Visit other markets to see new trends. Attend local trade meetings if possible. Learn from younger traders who understand social media and online selling. You do not have to copy everything, but you must be willing to try new things. Resilience is the final habit. Resilience means your business can survive shocks. Shocks include theft, illness, price spikes, currency changes, or a sudden drop in customers. To build resilience, do five things. First, keep an emergency fund. Even small daily savings add up. Second, avoid heavy debt. Borrow only for stock that you know will sell quickly. Third, diversify your income. If your shop sells only one product, a price crash can ruin you. Sell a mix of fast movers and a few higher-margin items. Fourth, build relationships with more than one supplier. If one fails, you have another. Fifth, take care of your health. A sick trader cannot open the shop. Rest when you can. Eat well. Drink clean water. Your business depends on you. Also, think about the future. Do you want to remain a small stall forever, or do you want to grow into a shop, then a wholesaler, then maybe a distributor? Write down your goal. Break it into small steps. Maybe this year you want to add a fridge to sell cold drinks. Next year you want to rent a bigger space. The year after you want to employ one assistant. Each step needs savings, planning, and discipline. Do not rush. Grow steadily. Finally, protect your reputation. In African trading communities, your name is your biggest asset. Pay your debts. Keep your promises. Sell honest goods. Treat people fairly. When you have a good name, suppliers trust you, customers return, and opportunities come. A good name cannot be stolen by a competitor. It is built day by day. In this module, you have learned to understand customers, select stock wisely, price for profit, manage cash, build relationships, market cheaply, keep records, plan ahead, adapt, and build resilience. These are the foundations of a successful small shop or market trading business. Apply them one at a time. Do not try to change everything in one day. Choose one habit this week, such as writing daily sales. Next week, add another, such as separating business and personal money. Small consistent steps will transform your business. Remember, you are not just selling goods. You are building a future for yourself, your family, and your community. Trade with pride, honesty, and skill. Thank you for completing Module 11. We wish you profitable trading and steady growth.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Module 11 Lesson 6: Practical Reference â Daily Trading Tools, Measures, and Safety Benchmarks

This lesson is a working reference sheet for small shop owners and market traders. It gathers the numbers, measures, and safety rules you need every day into one place: how to convert local measures to metric, how to read a stock sheet, how to set a break-even price, and how to keep food and chemicals safe for your customers. Keep it near your stall or print it for your records book. Every figure below comes from an official source so you can trust it when you negotiate with suppliers, calculate profit, or explain a decision to your family or business partner.

In African markets, trade rarely happens in neat metric units. Maize is sold by gorogoro (tins), rice by mudu or debe, tomatoes by the heap or basket, and cooking oil by the kibaba or litre bottle. Your profit is decided at the point where the measure you buy in meets the measure you sell in. If you do not know the exact conversion, you can lose money on every single sale without noticing. The tables and checklist below are designed to close that gap.

Table 1: Common African Market Measures and Metric Conversions

Use this table to convert what you buy into what you sell. Always confirm the local measure in your own market, because a gorogoro or mudu can vary by region and by trader.

Local measure Typical metric equivalent Common product Source / note
Gorogoro (paint tin, 4-litre) â 2.5â2.8 kg maize grain; â 2.0 kg beans Maize, beans, rice FAO/WFP market measure documentation; varies with moisture and grain type
Mudu (small tin) â 0.5â0.7 kg maize Maize, millet, sorghum Regional variation; weigh your own tin once and record it
Debe (20-litre tin) â 12â14 kg maize; â 18â20 L oil Maize, cooking oil FAO post-harvest handling guides
Kibaba (250 ml cup) 0.25 L Cooking oil, milk Standard East African measure
Heap / pile (tomatoes, onions) Varies: 0.5â2 kg Fresh vegetables Weigh 10 heaps and take the average for your pricing
Bunch (greens, bananas) Varies: 0.3â1.5 kg Sukuma wiki, spinach, matoke ILRI/FAO horticulture market studies
Litre bottle (reused soda bottle) â 0.5â1.0 L depending on bottle Oil, paraffin, milk Measure once with a graduated container and mark it

Source: Compiled from FAO, Post-harvest Losses and Food Waste resources, and ILRI, Market-oriented Smallholder Livestock and Crop Marketing briefs. Local measures vary â always verify with your own scale.

Table 2: Break-Even and Safety Benchmarks for Common Shop Items

This table shows typical wholesale-to-retail margins and the safety temperature or storage rule that applies. Margins are indicative for small informal retail in East and West Africa and will differ by city, season, and supplier.

Product Typical retail margin Storage / safety rule Source
Maize flour (1 kg) 8â15% Keep dry, off floor, away from chemicals; use within 3 months FAO cereal storage guidance
Cooking oil (1 L) 10â20% Store away from sunlight; do not reuse oil more than 2â3 times WHO healthy diet guidance
Fresh milk (1 L) 15â25% Keep below 4 Â°C if refrigerated; boil before sale if unpasteurised FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius
Eggs (tray of 30) 10â18% Store at 7â20 Â°C, pointed end down, do not wash before sale Aviagen Egg Handling Guide
Poultry meat (1 kg) 15â25% Keep chilled below 4 Â°C or frozen below â18 Â°C; cook to 74 Â°C internal FAO/WHO Codex; Aviagen processing guides
Animal health products (e.g. dewormer) 20â35% Store per label; keep locked and away from food; check expiry monthly MSD Animal Health product handling guidance
Soap and household chemicals 15â30% Never store above or beside food; keep in original labelled container WHO chemical safety guidance
Rice (1 kg) 8â15% Keep dry and covered; check for weevils weekly FAO rice storage guidance

Source: Margins compiled from FAO agricultural market information and ILRI smallholder market briefs; storage and safety rules from FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius, Aviagen egg and poultry handling guides, and MSD Animal Health product literature.

â  RED SAFETY WARNING â FOOD, CHEMICALS, AND ANIMAL HEALTH PRODUCTS

Never store pesticides, paraffin, veterinary drugs, or cleaning chemicals in the same container, shelf, or room as food, cooking oil, or animal feed. Poisoning of customers and family members is one of the most common and most preventable tragedies in small retail.

  • Keep all chemicals in their original labelled containers. Never use soda bottles or food tins for chemicals.
  • Wash hands with soap after handling chemicals, money, or raw meat, and before handling ready-to-eat food.
  • Do not sell expired, swollen, or damaged canned goods, milk, or drugs. Check expiry dates every week.
  • If a customer reports illness after buying your food, stop selling that batch immediately and report to your local public health officer.
  • For animal drugs, follow the withdrawal period on the label â selling meat or milk too soon after treatment can harm consumers and is illegal in most countries.

Sources: WHO Five Keys to Safer Food; FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius; MSD Animal Health withdrawal period guidance.

Quick Reference Checklist for Daily Trading

  1. Weigh your measures once a month. Confirm that your gorogoro, mudu, or debe still matches the weight you recorded, so you know your real cost per kilogram.
  2. Write the buying price and selling price on every product. If you cannot state your margin per unit, you are trading blind.
  3. Count cash at opening and closing. Record total sales, total expenses, and cash on hand in your notebook every day.
  4. Check expiry dates weekly. Remove expired goods from the shelf and record the loss so you can avoid over-ordering next time.
  5. Separate food from chemicals and money from stock. Use different shelves, boxes, or rooms.
  6. Keep a customer credit list. Write the name, amount, and date for every credit sale, and follow up weekly.
  7. Reinvest a fixed share of profit. Decide a percentage (for example 30%) to restock and a percentage to save for emergencies.
  8. Review your top five products monthly. Identify which items bring the most profit per unit and which take up space without selling.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Small-scale food retailing and market hygiene: https://www.fao.org/food-safety/en/
  • WHO â Five Keys to Safer Food Manual: https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241594639
  • ILRI â Market-oriented smallholder guides and briefs: https://www.ilri.org/publications
  • Aviagen â Egg Handling and Poultry Processing Guides: https://www.aviagen.com
  • MSD Animal Health â Product handling and withdrawal period guidance: https://www.msd-animal-health.com

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a daily cash-up procedure in a small shop?
options: A) To compare recorded sales with actual cash and card takings
B) To order new stock for the next day
C) To advertise upcoming promotions
D) To clean the shop floor
quiz.explanation: A cash-up checks that recorded sales match the money actually taken, helping detect errors or theft.

quiz.q: Which pricing method adds a fixed percentage to the cost price of goods?
options: A) Loss leader pricing
B) Markup pricing
C) Penetration pricing
D) Psychological pricing
quiz.explanation: Markup pricing adds a set percentage to the cost price to determine the selling price.

quiz.q: Why is stock rotation important for a market trader selling perishable goods?
options: A) It increases the number of suppliers
B) It removes the need for receipts
C) It reduces waste and keeps goods fresh
D) It allows higher taxes to be charged
quiz.explanation: Rotating stock so older items sell first reduces spoilage and waste, especially for perishables.

quiz.q: What does a gross profit margin measure?
options: A) Total sales before any costs
B) The amount of cash in the till
C) The number of items sold per day
D) The difference between sales and cost of goods sold
quiz.explanation: Gross profit margin is sales revenue minus the cost of goods sold, showing profit before other expenses.

quiz.q: Which record is most useful for tracking which products sell best?
options: A) A sales ledger or sales summary
B) A staff holiday roster
C) A supplier phone list
D) A shop decoration plan
quiz.explanation: A sales ledger or summary shows quantities and values sold, revealing best-selling products.

quiz.q: What is a key benefit of accepting mobile payments in a small market stall?
options: A) It removes the need for a business licence
B) It can increase sales by offering customer convenience
C) It guarantees lower supplier prices
D) It eliminates all transaction fees
quiz.explanation: Mobile payments add convenience for customers, which can attract more sales.

quiz.q: Which action best helps a small trader manage limited storage space?
options: A) Buying the largest possible stock quantities
B) Storing all goods in one mixed pile
C) Using stackable containers and clear labelling
D) Keeping only seasonal decorations in storage
quiz.explanation: Stackable containers and clear labels make the best use of limited space and speed up stock handling.

quiz.q: Why should a market trader keep a simple record of daily expenses?
options: A) To increase the number of customers
B) To avoid paying any tax
C) To replace the need for sales records
D) To understand true profit and control costs
quiz.explanation: Recording expenses shows true profit and helps identify where costs can be reduced.
